title: The Temptation and the Fall
setting: Eden: the river’s hidden channel at night, then the garden from dawn to the afternoon after the Fall
summary: Satan returns to Eden by night and hides inside a sleeping serpent. In the morning Eve persuades Adam to let her work alone; the serpent finds her, flatters her, and talks her into eating the forbidden fruit. Adam, horrified, eats too rather than lose her, and the pair fall into lust, shame and bitter mutual blame.

sections.title: The poet turns to tragedy
sections.note: Milton drops the friendly talk of angels and men and announces a tragic subject. He argues that patience and martyrdom are a truer heroism than the battles and tournaments of older epics.

sections.title: Satan’s return and his choice of the serpent
sections.note: After seven nights circling the earth in darkness, Satan slips back into Paradise through the underground channel of the Tigris. He settles on the serpent as the best disguise, since no one would wonder at cleverness in the subtlest beast.

sections.title: Satan’s soliloquy; he enters the serpent
sections.note: Satan admires the earth as a second, better Heaven, then admits that every beauty only deepens his torment. He hates his own ‘foul descent’ into a beast, but revenge wins, and he slides into the sleeping snake’s mouth.

sections.title: Eve proposes working apart
sections.note: At dawn Eve points out that the garden grows faster than two people can tend it. She suggests they divide their work, since together they keep stopping to talk and smile.

sections.title: The quarrel over separation
sections.note: Adam fears the enemy will catch her alone; Eve is hurt that he doubts her firmness and asks what faith is worth if never tested. Their exchange is loving but strained, and Adam finally lets her go with ‘Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more.’

sections.title: Eve leaves Adam’s side
sections.note: Eve withdraws her hand from his and goes off like a wood nymph or a goddess of gardens. The narrator breaks in to mourn: she will never again find sweet repast or sound repose in Paradise.

sections.title: The serpent finds Eve alone
sections.note: Satan finds Eve among the roses, herself the ‘fairest unsupported flower.’ For a moment her beauty leaves him ‘stupidly good,’ disarmed of his hate, until the Hell within him returns and he hardens his purpose.

sections.title: The serpent’s approach
sections.note: The serpent glides toward her upright on gleaming coils, the loveliest snake that ever was. He weaves and bows to catch her eye, like a ship tacking toward harbour.

sections.title: Flattery and the tale of the fruit
sections.note: The serpent hails Eve as a goddess who deserves worship from angels. Asked how a beast can speak, he claims that eating the fruit of a certain tree gave him reason and speech.

sections.title: To the forbidden tree
sections.note: Eve asks to see the tree, and the serpent leads her, glowing like a will-o’-the-wisp leading a traveller into a bog. When she sees which tree it is, she tells him God has forbidden it.

sections.title: The great temptation speech
sections.note: Rising like a classical orator, the serpent argues that he ate and lives, that God cannot justly punish the pursuit of knowledge, and that the ban is only meant to keep them low. Each step sounds reasonable; the whole is a tissue of lies.

sections.title: Eve eats
sections.note: Hungry at noon, Eve reasons herself into it and eats; ‘Earth felt the wound.’ Giddy with the fruit, she wonders whether to keep her new knowledge to herself, then decides Adam must share her fate, half from love and half from fear he might find another Eve.

sections.title: Adam meets the fallen Eve
sections.note: Adam, carrying a garland he made for her, meets Eve with the fruit in her hand. The garland drops, and in a silent speech to himself he resolves at once to die with her: ‘flesh of flesh, bone of my bone thou art.’

sections.title: Adam eats
sections.note: Adam reasons aloud that perhaps the offence is not so heinous, and tells Eve his lot is fixed with hers. She weeps for joy at his love; he eats ‘not deceived, but fondly overcome with female charm,’ and nature groans a second time.

sections.title: Lust, sleep and shame
sections.note: The fruit first inflames them with lust, and they make love on a flowery bank. They wake to find their eyes opened and their minds darkened, and Adam cries for the forests to hide him from the face of God.

sections.title: Fig leaves and mutual blame
sections.note: They cover themselves with the broad leaves of the banyan fig, but storms of anger and suspicion rise within. Adam blames Eve for wandering; Eve blames Adam for letting her go, and the book ends with no end to their quarrel.

famous.why: Milton’s redefinition of heroism, ‘the better fortitude of patience and heroick martyrdom,’ sets the terms for the rest of the poem.
The simile of a city dweller escaping into the countryside on a summer morning is one of the freshest images in the poem, and it is Satan’s pleasure it describes.
Satan ‘stupidly good’ for a moment before Eve’s beauty: a rare glimpse of the angel he was.
The Fall itself, told in a few plain words, with the whole of nature sighing ‘that all was lost.’
Adam’s private decision to fall with Eve, echoing Genesis, is the poem’s most moving and most argued-over moment.
Milton’s precise verdict on Adam, ‘not deceived, but fondly overcome with female charm,’ separates his sin from Eve’s.

themes: True heroism lies in patience and obedience rather than in battle.
Freedom requires the possibility of failure: Adam will not force Eve to stay.
Persuasion works by mixing truths with lies until the lie sounds like reason.
Love and self-giving, the best things in Adam, become the means of his fall.
art: The serpent rising upright on shining coils among the roses, its crested head bowed toward Eve as she reaches for the fruit.
